builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?
summary: CoEvoBench replaces separate, single-component agent evaluations with a joint benchmark in which an LLM researcher iteratively decides whether to modify the model or the harness under a 24-hour compute budget. Running it costs substantial frontier-model API usage plus training compute within that budget, which is beyond a single 24 GB GPU setup. Its central finding is a failure mode: LLM researchers produce a strong first improvement but cannot convert feedback from the improved system into further gains, so co-evolution pipelines built on this premise will plateau quickly.
rationale: CoEvoBench is an evaluation benchmark for LLM-driven model-harness co-evolution, not a deployable method, and its 24-hour training loop over multiple domains exceeds the reader's infrastructure, so its value is limited to interpreting vendor claims about recursive self-improvement.

claims.statement: CoEvoBench replaces separate, single-component agent evaluations with a joint benchmark in which an LLM researcher iteratively decides whether to modify the model or the harness under a 24-hour compute budget. Running it costs substantial frontier-model API usage plus training compute within that budget, which is beyond a single 24 GB GPU setup. Its central finding is a failure mode: LLM researchers produce a strong first improvement but cannot convert feedback from the improved system into further gains, so co-evolution pipelines built on this premise will plateau quickly.

The strongest evaluated LLM researcher closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system within a 24-hour budget; co-evolution succeeds on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding.
